query_database.py:181-192: the only path to the try/finally that calls entry.lock.release() (191) is after `await entry.lock.acquire()` returned (182); any exception during acquire (including cancellation) goes to the except at 183-186, which does not release the lock, only the registry claim. So release is reached only by the acquiring task, and exactly once. CPython asyncio.Lock.acquire appends waiters to a FIFO deque and its fast path is skipped while non-cancelled waiters exist, so there is no barging. release wakes the first waiter, so same-id calls run in acquire-call order. A task cancelled after being woken passes the lock on to the next waiter, so ordering holds. Based on my knowledge of the CPython stdlib; I did not read the stdlib source in this environment.

But the final sentence at cleanup-error-handling.md:41 ('cleanup in the finally: still runs on that same thread, before the exception surfaces at the await') is wrong in the very scenario the paragraph discusses: a cancelled request. With asyncio.to_thread, cancelling the awaiting task raises CancelledError at the await immediately while the worker thread keeps running the query; the thread's finally runs only later, when the query ends. Mechanism is correct: asyncio's default executor is a ThreadPoolExecutor, and concurrent.futures.thread's atexit hook (_python_exit) plus loop.shutdown_default_executor join its worker threads, so a blocked worker delays exit (each wait is also capped by release.wait(timeout=30)).
